the deposition of handprints can result in the transfer of DNA from one hand to another, and this can be detected in subsequent contacts with surfaces and objects.

DNA deposited through handshaking can be detected on surfaces subsequently contacted by the opposing person, but the detection rate is influenced by the relative shedding ability of individuals, the number of surfaces contacted and the time between the handshake and deposition.

the detection of DNA transferred indirectly via hand contact, and highlights the factors influencing the transfer of DNA from one individual to another, and its persistence on contacted items.
the persistence of DNA on surfaces, the influence of activities on the transfer of DNA, and the potential for DNA to be transferred via a secondary source.
the persistence of non-self DNA deposited on the hands of an opposing hand-shaker and the influence of various factors on its detection.

the DNA detected on a surface is most likely from the person who deposited the item, but that DNA from a secondary person or source may be present, and that its detection may be influenced by a variety of factors.

DNA transfer and persistence is highly variable and influenced by a range of factors, including the activities performed and the individuals involved.
the persistence of DNA on a surface, and the likelihood of its detection, is dependent on the deposition and subsequent handling of the item by the individual.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the detection of a secondary contributor to a DNA transfer event, such as the opposing hand-shaking individual, is not guaranteed, and that the detection of both parties involved in the event is highly variable.

the detection of DNA deposited by a secondary person on a surface contacted by a depositor is not only possible, but can be affected by the relative DNA shedding abilities of the individuals involved, as well as by the number of items contacted and the activities performed by each individual.
